But for all the boldness of the reimagining, and the stellar track record of so much of the cast, “Death of a Salesman” is a disappointment in several ways.
Thanks to Clarke’s heartbreaking brilliance, the role of Linda is finally given her due.
All in all, you are unlikely ever to see a finer production of Death of a Salesman than this one.

Of course, Linda's efforts are just as doomed as Willy's pursuits, and Clarke's layered performance recasts Death of a Salesman as a dual tragedy, with Linda as a hidden crux of the show to whom attention must truly be paid.
Nevertheless, this Salesman is a production for the ages, and one I cannot recommend enough.

But in the end, the play’s new Broadway revival, which originated at London’s Theatre and stars Wendell Pierce (“The Wire”) and Sharon D. Clarke (“Caroline, Or Change”) as Willy and Linda Loman, makes for an accessible, compelling, and distinctive re-envisioning.
This is a production that honors Miller's masterpiece while finding fresh insights in its familiar rhythms.
Yet far from overshadowing the play’s larger message, of the elusiveness of the American dream, these twists reinforce it.

Missteps aside, this Death of a Salesman offers up a vital, fresh take on an American classic, making it all the more American for its inclusiveness, and as classic as the towering performances of Wendell Pierce and Sharon D Clarke.

All of Willy’s joyous American Dream jingoism is odd to hear coming from a Willy Loman who’s African American, and the genius of Pierce’s performance is how he uses that optimism to highlight the character’s self-deception.

Unlike most other productions, this Linda sings; and in the final moment we are left with just Linda and her song in a downstage spotlight — an image more wrenching than anything you're likely to witness on Broadway this season.

Everything in the production seems pitched over the top, including Willy’s declining mental condition, which here feels more like full-blown dementia than merely a man defeated by life who is losing his grip.
But this Salesman seems not to have weathered the three years so well, losing a substantial slice of effectiveness on its journey from the Thames to the Hudson.

Whether Death of a Salesman is a text you’ve chewed through many times over or something you’re exposed to for the first time, this is an eye-opening revival.
In those moments, the cast rises to the occasion and this Death of a Salesman play truly soars.
In the play’s final moments, Clarke delivers a poignant requiem — the Great Migration poignantly distilled down to a moment that is at once full of mourning and survival.
If seeing previous productions of Death of a Salesman has inured you to Willy’s ultimate fate, this one should bring back the tears, and Clarke deserves a lot of credit for that difficult gift.
Race adds another dimension to this new version of the “Death of A Salesman,” a subtext while enhancing the bigger message.
The best thing about Miranda Cromwell's sometimes uncertain production is the opportunity it gives four lead actors to do strong, stunning, and, in some cases, highly original work.
Whether it’s the right casting, aside from the peerless Clarke in stand-by-your-man mode, is another matter entirely.
